notes.title: Start here: DevDeck's backup import, from file to database
notes.body:
DevDeck is an offline flashcard app (React, Zustand, and Dexie on top of the browser database IndexedDB). This pack studies one feature: restoring your progress from a JSON backup file. The code path is short: `importBackup` in `src/store.ts` reads the file, `validateImport` in `src/importValidation.ts` checks it, and `importData` in `src/db.ts` writes it.

Reading order, as the course README gives it:

1. `astraupskill/01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: the import trace.
2. `astraupskill/02-CONCEPTS.md`: eight short sections; most concept quizzes come from them.
3. `astraupskill/03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`: the annotated `importData`, the "predict, then run" table, and the regression tests.
4. `astraupskill/04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`.
5. `astraupskill/05-PRACTICE.md`: exercises 0-8, each with a Goal and a Check (the goal-check quizzes).
6. `astraupskill/06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md` and the trace lab.

Keep `src/importValidation.ts` and `src/db.ts` open side by side; both are short.

notes.title: Reading the validator: small helpers, one block per section
notes.body:
`validateImport` is about 85 lines, but it is built from a few tiny helper functions defined at the top (`object`, `text`, `number`, `integer`, `day`, `fail`). Learn those first; then each block below them reads like a checklist.

The function is organised in blocks: schema version, the two arrays, every review state, every review log, settings, and meta. Each block ends in `fail("...")` with its own name, so the error message tells you which block rejected the file (but not which record). The function stops at the first problem it finds.

To practise, take the "Predict, then run" table in chapter 3 and, for each edit, find the exact helper and line that decides it. That is Exercise 0, and it is the best preparation for the quizzes on this pack.

excerpts.quote: | `number(v, min, max)` | finite number in a range |
const fail = (field: string): never => { throw new Error(`Malformed backup: ${field}`); };
The function stops at the **first** problem and names only the block, not the record, so a user with 2,000 logs learns that one is bad but not which one.

notes.title: What a Dexie transaction is, in plain words
notes.body:
IndexedDB is the browser's built-in database; Dexie is a friendlier library on top of it. A **transaction** groups several reads and writes so they succeed or fail as one unit. In Dexie you write `db.transaction("rw", [tables...], async () => { ... })`: "rw" means read-write, the list names the tables the callback may touch, and the callback holds the work.

Before the quizzes, read `importData` in `src/db.ts` (lines 166-201) with a pencil. Mark which lines run *before* the transaction and which run *inside* it, and for each line inside it ask: if this line threw, which of the earlier lines' effects would survive? Look up in the Dexie docs what happens to a transaction whose callback throws, rather than guessing. Then read `saveReview` (lines 118-126), the same idea at a smaller scale.

**The tables listed on line 176 are the transaction's scope.** Touching a table not in that list inside the callback would fail.

notes.title: `as ExportData` does nothing when the program runs
notes.body:
**Key: nothing at runtime, as the cast is erased and code may read fields the file never had.**

`as ExportData` is a TypeScript *type assertion*: it tells the compiler "trust me, this is an ExportData". When TypeScript compiles to JavaScript, all types are removed, so the line becomes plain `JSON.parse(text)`. Whatever the file contained is now *typed* as `ExportData`, and the compiler will let you read `payload.reviewStates[0].ease` even if the file has no `reviewStates`. That is why a separate runtime validator exists.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Coerces field types*: a cast changes no values; `"5"` stays a string.
- *Strips unknown properties*: nothing is removed; `JSON.parse` keeps every key.
- *Throws a TypeError for a missing property*: no check runs, so nothing can throw because of the type.

excerpts.quote: const payload = JSON.parse(text) as ExportData;
TypeScript types are erased at compile time, so that line produces exactly the same JavaScript as `JSON.parse(text)`.

notes.title: A validator should match what the app can actually produce
notes.body:
**Key: rules not derived from the producer accept values the app cannot emit, and may reject ones it can.**

The scheduler is the *producer* of `ease` values: it never goes below 1.3 and "Easy" adds 0.15 with no upper limit. The validator allows 1-10, a range nobody worked out from the scheduler. So `ease: 1.0` passes although the app can never make it, and in theory a card graded Easy 51 times would reach 10.15 and its backup would be refused. The guide's lesson: "the validator exists" is not the same as "the validator matches the domain".

Why the others are wrong:
- *The scheduler is buggy; clamp to 10*: the guide does not call it a bug and notes 10.15 would take decades; the point is the mismatch.
- *Loosen to any positive ease*: that widens the gap instead of deriving rules from the producer.
- *Exploitable to skip reviews*: the guide says none of these cases causes a crash or harm.

excerpts.quote: The scheduler never goes below 1.3 (`MIN_EASE`, `scheduler.ts:11`), so `ease: 1.0` is accepted although the app cannot produce it.
They are worth knowing because they show the difference between "the validator exists" and "the validator matches the domain".

notes.title: Why every other schema version is refused today
notes.body:
**Key: with no migration code, other versions have an unknown shape; later, migrate step by step, then validate.**

`SCHEMA_VERSION` is 1, and the first validator check fails any payload whose `schemaVersion` is different. The app has no code that understands version 0 or version 2, so it cannot say what such a file contains; rejecting is the only claim it can honestly make. When the format changes, the guide's pattern is a `migrate(payload)` step that upgrades one version at a time and then runs the current validator.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Dexie's version().stores() migrates backups*: that versions the IndexedDB tables, not the backup file; they are separate systems.
- *Newer versions import unchanged*: nothing guarantees future versions only add fields.
- *Warn and accept, version is advisory*: accepting an unknown shape is what the check exists to prevent.

excerpts.quote: if (!object(payload) || payload.schemaVersion !== SCHEMA_VERSION) fail("unsupported schema version");

When the format changes, the pattern is a `migrate(payload)` step that upgrades one version at a time and then calls the current validator. Note that this is separate from Dexie's own `this.version(1).stores(...)` (`db.ts:29`), which versions the IndexedDB schema, not the backup file.

notes.title: Unknown deck ids are kept, and nothing breaks
notes.body:
**Key: it is kept: deck ids just need to be strings, and its counter just stays empty.**

For `enabledDeckIds`, the validator only checks `s.enabledDeckIds.every(text)`: each entry must be a non-empty string of at most 200 characters. It never checks the id against the real decks. `importData` filters unknown *card* ids but writes settings as given, so `"no-such-deck"` is stored. Nothing crashes: the per-deck counter code creates an empty counter for each enabled id, and no card matches it.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Fails with 'Malformed backup: settings'*: a string passes `text`, so the settings block accepts it.
- *Dropped by the known-ids filter*: that filter (`knownIds`) is built from cards and applied only to states and logs.
- *Crashes the stats screen*: the guide says an empty counter is created and "Nothing breaks".

excerpts.quote: !Array.isArray(s.enabledDeckIds) || !s.enabledDeckIds.every(text)
Nothing breaks: `getPerDeckCounts` creates an empty counter for each enabled id (`src/queue.ts:174-176`), and no card matches it.

notes.title: What `asserts payload is ExportData` buys you
notes.body:
**Key: the result can't be ignored, as it throws or returns, and after a return the payload's type is narrowed.**

An *assertion function* has two possible outcomes: it throws, or it returns normally. A caller cannot forget to check a result, because there is no result to check: if the payload is bad, execution never gets past the call. And after a normal return, TypeScript treats `payload` as `ExportData`, so the following code type-checks without a cast. A function returning `true`/`false` can be called and its answer ignored.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The check moves to compile time*: the checks are ordinary runtime code; only the narrowing is a compile-time effect.
- *It may repair the payload*: the validator only throws or returns; the practice guide says "the validator throws, it does not transform".
- *Tree-shaken out of production*: it is called by `importData`, so it ships and runs.

excerpts.quote: it either throws or returns normally, and after a normal return TypeScript treats `payload` as `ExportData`. That is a stronger contract than returning `true`/`false`: a caller cannot forget to look at the result, because a bad payload never gets past the call.
export function validateImport( payload: unknown, ): asserts payload is ExportData {

notes.title: Unknown cards are filtered and missing ones recreated
notes.body:
**Key: states and logs of unknown cards are filtered, and missing bundled cards get fresh states.**

Cards ship inside the app, so a backup from an older build can mention cards this build no longer has. `importData` builds `knownIds` from the bundled cards and keeps only states (line 172) and logs (line 188) whose `cardId` is known. Inside the transaction it then finds every bundled card that got no state from the file and adds a fresh state for it with `createNewReviewState`. The regression test pins all three behaviours.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The file is rejected*: the policy is "filter, don't fail".
- *New cards stay stateless until reviewed*: lines 181-184 create their states during the import.
- *Imported as orphans, cleaned up later*: unknown states never reach the database.

excerpts.quote: const knownIds = new Set(allCards.map((c) => c.id)); const states = payload.reviewStates.filter((s) => knownIds.has(s.cardId));
const missing = allCards .filter((c) => !restored.has(c.id)) .map((c) => createNewReviewState(c.id, now));

notes.title: clear() then bulkAdd() is safe only inside the transaction
notes.body:
**Key: both run in one readwrite transaction, so any failure after clear aborts and restores the tables.**

`clear()` deletes every review state. If the next step failed and nothing undid the delete, the user would be left with no progress. Here both calls are inside the `db.transaction("rw", ...)` callback. If `bulkAdd` (or anything later in the callback) fails, Dexie aborts the transaction, and IndexedDB restores all four tables to how they were before it began. The worked-change chapter lists this as point 3.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The validator guarantees bulkAdd cannot fail*: validation catches bad data, not a full disk or a closed tab.
- *clear() returns a snapshot*: it returns nothing used for rollback; the database does the rollback.
- *Dexie defers the deletes*: the rows are cleared; it is the transaction abort that brings them back.

excerpts.quote: await db.reviewStates.clear(); await db.reviewStates.bulkAdd(states);
**`clear()` then `bulkAdd()` is safe only because of the transaction.** Outside one, a failure after `clear()` would leave the user with no progress at all.

notes.title: The day helper's round-trip catches February 30
notes.body:
**Key: rollover dates like 2025-02-30, which parse into March, so the re-formatted string differs.**

`2025-02-30` passes the `YYYY-MM-DD` regex, and `Date.parse('2025-02-30')` gives a real timestamp in V8, because the engine rolls the extra days over into March. So the first two checks pass. The third check formats the parsed date back (`toISOString().slice(0, 10)`) and gets `2025-03-02`, which is not equal to the input, so the value is rejected. Only that comparison exposes a calendar date that does not exist.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Dates before 1970*: negative timestamps format back correctly; the helper is about impossible dates.
- *Two-digit years*: the regex already requires four digits, so they never reach the third check.
- *Timezone offsets*: a bare `YYYY-MM-DD` is parsed as UTC and formatted as UTC, so it round-trips unchanged.

excerpts.quote: /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(v) && Number.isFinite(Date.parse(v)) && new Date(v).toISOString().slice(0, 10) === v);
`Date.parse('2025-02-30')` is a valid timestamp in V8 (it rolls over into March), so the helper formats the parsed date back and requires it to equal the input (line 19).

notes.title: Why imported review logs lose their ids
notes.body:
**Key: logs use auto-increment keys, so file ids could collide with keys Dexie assigns to later reviews.**

Review logs are an append-only history whose primary key is a number Dexie assigns automatically, counting up. If the import kept the ids from the file, those numbers might not line up with Dexie's own counter, and a key Dexie generates for a later review could collide with an imported one. So `importData` removes `id` from each log with `const { id: _id, ...rest } = l` and lets Dexie assign fresh keys. (Settings and meta keep fixed ids like `"settings"`.)

Why the others are wrong:
- *Dexie refuses explicit keys*: the guide's reason is collisions, not a Dexie rule.
- *Smaller rows, faster import*: one number per row makes no meaningful difference.
- *The validator already rejects logs with ids*: the log block never checks `id`, so logs with ids pass.

excerpts.quote: const { id: _id, ...rest } = l; void _id; return rest;
**Old log ids are stripped** (lines 189-193) so Dexie assigns fresh auto-increment keys. Re-using ids from a file could collide with keys Dexie generates later.

notes.title: Two states for one card: rejected by the seen-ids set
notes.body:
**Key: it is rejected as 'Malformed backup: review state': a Set of seen ids trips on the repeat.**

The review-state loop keeps a `Set` called `ids`. For each state it checks `ids.has(s.cardId)` among its conditions, then adds the id. The first copy passes and is added; the second copy finds its id already in the set, so the condition fails and `fail("review state")` throws. This happens in validation, before the transaction, so nothing is written.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The later state wins via put()*: states are written with `bulkAdd`, and the file never gets that far.
- *Both written, then ConstraintError*: that is what would happen *without* the set: `bulkAdd` would throw mid-transaction, which is safe but gives a confusing error.
- *Silently filtered like unknown cards*: the unknown-card filter is about ids not in the bundle; a duplicate of a known card is rejected.

excerpts.quote: const ids = new Set<string>(); for (const s of p.reviewStates) { if ( !object(s) || !text(s.cardId) || ids.has(s.cardId) ||
| duplicate the first state | | `Malformed backup: review state` |

notes.title: Validation and the transaction guard different failures
notes.body:
**Key: validation stops bad data before storage is touched; the transaction covers quota errors or crashes.**

There are two kinds of failure. A file can be *bad data*: a negative `due`, a duplicate state. Validation (line 170, before the transaction) catches these, so IndexedDB is never touched. Or the data can be fine but the *write* fails: storage quota exceeded, a bug in the callback, the tab closing mid-write. Validation cannot see those; the transaction (lines 174-199) rolls them back. Each layer guards something the other cannot.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The transaction is for speed*: its job in this code is all-or-nothing replacement.
- *Validating inside would deadlock*: the guide gives no such reason; validating first simply means nothing needs rolling back.
- *Either alone would suffice*: the guide says validation alone leaves write failures exposed, and the transaction alone lets well-formed garbage in.

excerpts.quote: Validation catches bad **data**. The transaction catches failures that have nothing to do with the data: a storage quota error, a bug in the callback, the tab being closed mid-write.

notes.title: Why the rejection test also compares the stored data
notes.body:
**Key: code that writes first and validates afterwards, where a rejection-only assertion would still pass.**

The promise of the change is "a bad file changes nothing". Checking only that the import rejects proves the error path exists. But imagine a buggy version that writes the file to the database and *then* validates: it would still reject, so a rejection-only test passes, yet the user's progress is already overwritten. Re-exporting and deep-comparing states, settings and meta with the original catches exactly that.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Mutations leaking between cases*: `structuredClone(original)` per case handles that, not the comparison.
- *The wrong error message*: that is Exercise 1's concern; today the tests only match `/Malformed backup/`.
- *Flaky async ordering*: the tests `await` the rejection; the comparison is about stored data.

excerpts.quote: After each rejection it re-exports and compares `reviewStates`, `settings` and `meta` to the original. That second half is what proves "nothing changed". A test that only checked the rejection would pass even if the code wrote first and validated afterwards.
